speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: WHEAT, OATS AND BARLEY    ANNOUNCEMENT OF INITIAL PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a statement about Canadian wheat board initial prices to producers for western wheat, oats and barley for the crop year beginning August 1, 1963. These are being fixed at $1.50 per bushel for No. 1 Manitoba northern, basis in store Fort William-Port Arthur or Vancouver; 60 cents per bushel for 2 C.W. oats, basis in store Fort William-Port Arthur; 96 cents per bushel for 3 C.W. six-row barley, basis in store Fort William-Port Arthur. These are the same levels as for these grades during the crop year which is now drawing to a close. Initial prices for other grades of western wheat, oats and barley will be announced later by the Canadian wheat board. Although the government takes full responsibility for the level of initial prices, under the Canadian Wheat Board Act the Canadian wheat board was, as is customary, asked to make its recommendations which were in accord with the government's decision.
Before reaching its decision on initial prices and on other aspects of the government's program which I shall refer to later, the government made a careful reassessment of the rapidly changing grain situation, and consulted not only with the Canadian wheat board but with a number of farm leaders from the prairies. Taking into consideration the stocks on hand, the record grain crop that appears likely to be produced on the prairies this year, the uncertainties created by the results of the United States farm referendum, and the negotiations now going on in Geneva under the auspices of GATT for new international arrangements for the marketing of cereals, the government came to the view that the initial prices should remain unchanged for the coming year. The government shares the opinion of major farm organizations that efforts should be concentrated on moving as much grain as possible.
There are two sides to this matter of our wheat marketing, supply and demand. Taking one year with another and a variation in yields which must be expected, we should aim to avoid the production of unmanageable surpluses and through appropriate crop diversification be in a position to meet changing domestic and foreign demand for wheat, coarse grains and livestock. Our production policies, including the various programs affecting wheat and other grains, must be designed to achieve these objectives. The government has initiated a review of these policies and programs to determine in what way they might be adjusted to achieve a better balance in agricultural production and the avoidance of burdensome surpluses. For example, the government considers that we should be in a better position than we are at present to meet the expected increase in demand for livestock and feed grains. On the demand side, the government is making every effort to help the wheat board to increase to the maximum commercial sales in markets throughout the world, wherever they are to be found.
The government has decided that the time has come to move forward on another front which should prove of both short run and long run advantage to western wheat producers. To help meet the food needs of the developing countries, Canada for many years now has been making wheat and flour available as part of our Colombo plan assistance. I wish to announce at this time the intention of the government to ask parliament to provide for a program of supplying wheat or wheat flour to international agencies, including the world food program, and to developing countries which are not now commercial markets or where commercial exports are limited by capacity to pay. Something can be done this year. The intention is on a progressive basis to increase the amount of Canadian food aid in appropriate relationship to the total of our assistance activities. It is expected that the total allocation for this purpose might rise to a level of around $40 million per annum over the course of the next few years.
The actual amount of wheat and flour to be made available for assistance purposes in the next crop year will depend on the needs of the world food program and the absorptive capacity of the developing countries we wish to assist. Safeguards will be introduced to ensure that the provision of additional Canadian wheat and flour does not interfere with
2560	HOUSE OF
Announcement of Initial Grain Prices the normal commercial marketings of Canada and other exporting countries whom we shall be consulting as appropriate. I am confident all members of the house will agree that food aid, in particular the provision of wheat and flour which we are so well placed to produce, should be a continuing and important part of our external development assistance programs as long as the need for food exists.
This enlarged program of food aid, in combination with the efforts that are being made to maintain and increase commercial sales, to gain access to import markets and to stabilize international trade at reasonable prices, seems to the government to represent the right approach to the problems that confront western grain producers under present circumstances. I feel confident it is an approach that will commend itself to western producers and to hon. members on all sides of the house.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: WHEAT, OATS AND BARLEY    ANNOUNCEMENT OF INITIAL PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I listened to the unveiling of this plan I could not but recollect that when we were in office we were criticized for assistance by way of wheat, grain, flour and the like to needy countries. I, and all hon. members of this party, are very happy at the conversion of those in the Liberal party who previously held the very reverse of the opinion inherent in the announcement today.
It will be recalled that we gave strong support to the setting up of an international food bank in order to provide assistance and aid to needy countries, and at the same time to permit the setting aside of surpluses which otherwise would hang over the market price. Furthermore, we greatly expanded assistance under the Colombo plan to nations within the commonwealth. We increased this aid from $30 million to about $50 million. Last year, by reason of special circumstances, we reduced that amount, but it was still approximately $7J million or $10 million more than had been the case when we came into office.
The minister also made reference to the need to expand our markets, and we are also in accord with that. We recall so well that during the days of the previous Liberal government the then minister of trade and commerce stated "If they want our wheat let them come and get it." That was not the attitude of the government of which I had the honour to be head. We expanded our markets, and we are now glad to hear that the present government intends to follow in our footsteps and will make available the


necessary credits to those nations which because of their peculiar economic conditions would be unable to make the required purchases.
I have nothing to say in regard to the initial price. The ultimate determination as to whether what is being done is worth while so far as the farmer is concerned will await the final payment, which will indicate the actual price the farmer will be receiving. However, I am sure no one will be surprised when I express the view that the western farmer will be taken aback at the complete failure of the government to carry out one of its major agricultural promises-

maintopic: WHEAT, OATS AND BARLEY    ANNOUNCEMENT OF INITIAL PRICES
speechtext: Commitment.

maintopic: WHEAT, OATS AND BARLEY    ANNOUNCEMENT OF INITIAL PRICES
speechtext: -"commitment" is the word, whereby it undertook to pay $3 per bushel for the initial unit of 300 bushels. That seems to have joined the ranks of the forgotten promises, as well as the promise of a floor of $2 a bushel. It was singularly absent from the announcement made by the minister, and indicates that these two promises of $3 for the first 300 bushels and a $2 floor have joined the ranks of the forgotten promises of a few months ago.

maintopic: WHEAT, OATS AND BARLEY    ANNOUNCEMENT OF INITIAL PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in this group welcome the announcement that has just been made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce respecting the initial prices to be paid for wheat, but I think that welcome will have to be confined to the fact that it was announced a little earlier this year than it was last year. It is exactly the same as it was last year and, as the Leader of the Opposition has just pointed out, it appears to be a major retreat from the promises that were held out to the western farmers, first of all for $3 a bushel on the initial quota; and in so far as the $2 a bushel is concerned, being the floor price that was promised, I suppose we will have to wait and see what the final payment will be before we pass judgment.
I hope that the efforts of the Canadian wheat board in selling wheat and wheat flour in the international market will be supported by the government in allowing the wheat board to be more competitive; that is, to offer more competitive terms, which I think all hon. members realize are necessary in the international wheat market today. Credit, of course, is one of the very important terms that must be offered if we are to be competitive. Of course there are other things as well that should be taken into consideration.
The minister pointed out that there is a need for balancing the production of farm products; that is, to try to shift some of the emphasis to livestock products, for which

he suggested there is a demand. I suggest to him that this may be well so until we reach the point where we have a surplus in this area of farm production also. While the beef industry particularly is the only part of farm production that is in a healthy position today, I suggest to him this is so because there has not been overproduction of this product. It seems to me it is rather important that we consider keeping a healthy industry healthy.
Regarding the matter of offering food in the form of wheat and wheat flour to countries as aid, I would say on behalf of this party that we welcome this program. We have suggested over the years that this is an area to which the Canadian government should really be paying a little more attention. I hope when they do make these offers they will take into consideration the depressed condition of the flour milling industry across Canada and perhaps put a little more emphasis on offering the product that is processed in Canada rather than the raw material, which has been the case in the past. I might also say in closing that we were a little perturbed about the cut made in the Colombo plan last year by the previous government. We are happy to see that the government is moving into this food aid program even though it may be in a different channel.

speechtext:
Certainly that would be a very apt description of what is being proffered today. I would have hoped the minister would say something about the very definite commitment made to prairie farmers by the Prime Minister in his statement in Saskatoon on March 6 last. That commitment involved two things. It involved first of all a guaranteed payment of $2 a bushel for wheat, basis Fort William; it also involved a two price system for wheat under which the wheat consumed in Canada would be estimated on the equated price and the extra money would be paid to the farmers on their initial delivery quota.
The minister has made no mention of either of those commitments, nor has either the minister or the Prime Minister at any time said this is now accepted as part of the Liberal commitment and that if it is not going to be done now, it will be done in the
Announcement of Initial Grain Prices near future. The government has simply ignored its commitment, but I think it will not be allowed to forget it by the great bulk of the farmers of the prairie provinces.
With reference to the proposal that additional wheat and wheat flour should be given to emerging nations, I am sure this will have the support of the people of Canada. Certainly I can assure the government that it will have the support of the members of this party. At a time when we have surplus food in Canada one of the great weapons of democracy is to use this surplus food to help strengthen the emerging nations and help them in this period of transition through which they are now passing.
However, I do not think forty or fifty million dollars worth of wheat or wheat flour is going to solve our problems, and I hope the government will be giving some consideration to following the program which the United States has followed of making wheat available to countries who need it in exchange for foreign currency, or even on a barter basis, and certainly on a long term credit basis.
Unless this wheat can be moved it is going to create a very serious economic problem for the people of Canada. But the immediate problem, the problem to which I think the government ought to give its attention, is the price for the farmers. The bright promise which has been made by the government of a $2 a bushel guaranteed payment and a two price system is something to which we hope the government will give attention, and give assurance to the house that this will not be merely a forgotten promise.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce to the house the approval in principle by this government of the proposal of the government of Nova Scotia for the establishment of a new national park in Nova Scotia. This announcement is being made simultaneously by Hon. R. L. Stanfield, premier of Nova Scotia, for the government of Nova Scotia, and by myself and on behalf of my colleague the Minister of Labour for the government of Canada. At this time I want also to thank for their co-operation and assistance members of parliament from the province of Nova Scotia who sit both to your right and to your left.

The proposed national park is to be established at Kejimkujik lake in western Nova Scotia and becomes the first national park to be established since the creation of Terra Nova national park in Newfoundland in 1957. The proposed national park is 38 miles south of Annapolis Royal and 150 miles west of Halifax. It is considered to be an outstanding example of Nova Scotia's beauty of forest and sea. More than 20 lakes, some with excellent beach potential, and a number of connecting rivers are the heart of the park proposal. In addition to the lake area, a representative section of Nova Scotia's Atlantic shore line will be preserved as part of the new national park. Kejimkujik lake will be the site of the national park in Nova Scotia and the nineteenth national park in Canada. Cape Breton Highlands national park on Cape Breton island, Nova Scotia, was established in 1936.
On behalf of the people of Canada I wish to express our gratitude to the government of Nova Scotia for having made available, free from encumbrances, these scenic lands which will henceforward be dedicated to the people of Canada. Both this government and the government of Nova Scotia have proceeded as expeditiously as possible to settle the final details of the arrangements. We hope for a conclusion in the early months of this fall so that this important project can be placed in motion.
Hon. George C. Nowlan (Digby-Annapolis-
Kings): Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house will have been interested in the announcement just made by the minister, and that the members from Nova Scotia will have been delighted. He will understand, of course, from his reference to the name of Annapolis Royal that I have more than a mere academic interest in this matter. This is one of the decisions of the government of which I can fully approve. In fact this step may have been recommended by my colleague the former minister, and in that connection it adds to my interest.
This will be a great addition to the tourist industry of Nova Scotia. The selection is one which, sited as it is in an area in the southwestern part of the province, will have a great impact on various constituencies represented here, and one which the government of Nova Scotia have fully approved and recommended.
I commend the government for having proceeded in this way by bringing the proposal forward as soon as possible.

1.	Who recommended the parole of Mr. Leopold Dion of Pont Rouge, Quebec, sentenced to life imprisonment in 1940?
2.	What were the reasons given in support of this parole?
3.	At the end of 1962 or the beginning of 1963, who recommended a new parole for the same man?
4.	What were the reasons advanced in support of this parole?
5.	Will a general investigation be made of the national parole board?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As to questions 1, 2, 3 and 4 I must reply that it is not the policy to disclose information contained in parole files because of the confidential nature thereof. In order that the national parole board may receive as complete information as possible, both good and bad, from all possible sources, the policy is to regard all information and representations contained in such files as confidential. Nor is it the policy for the board to disclose the specific grounds of parole in an individual case.
In order, however, that hon. members may fully understand the situation, I should like to add the following.
Under the terms of the Parole Act the board, with exceptions which are not relevant here, "has exclusive jurisdiction and absolute discretion to grant, refuse to grant or revoke parole" (section 5). The act also provides that the board shall, at the times prescribed by the regulations, review the case of every inmate of a penitentiary serving a sentence of two years or more, "whether or not an application has been made by or on behalf of the inmate" (section 6). The regulations provide-as far as present purposes are concerned-that, in the case of an inmate serving a sentence of two years or more, the board shall review the case at least every two years.
Review of such cases by the board is therefore not dependant upon any representations being made to the board and any such representations, whether emanating from the inmate or his friends, are taken merely as indicating an active interest on his part in obtaining a parole.
Coming now to question No. 5 the answer is that no intention has been formed to direct a general investigation of the national parole board. I need hardly say with what horror

we all regard the deaths of the four boys in Quebec city, to which the question obviously relates, or what profound sympathy we feel for their families. I intend, however, to await the outcome of the police investigation and the inquests, and any subsequent court proceedings, before making any further comment on this tragic case, except to say that I made a point of examining the files of the national parole board and, whatever the merits of the decision to grant parole in this case, I find, as I had anticipated, that the case was considered painstakingly and in complete objectivity by the board.

1.	What success has been achieved by the government program for the extermination of lamprey in the great lakes?
2.	Does the federal government intend to continue this program and, if so, could the Minister of Fisheries bring the house up to date on its present operation?

1. In 1962 and 1963 in lake Superior, the experimental area, the number of adult marine lampreys was reduced by at least 80 per cent. With this reduction in numbers, wounding of lake trout has dropped, their availability-catch per given yardage of net-has increased and larger trout are appearing in the catches.
2. The program is being carried out in accordance with the terms of the great lakes fishery convention between Canada and the United States. This convention remains in force until October 1965. The convention provides for a joint review in the eighth year of the activities of the commission appointed pursuant thereto to determine the desirability of continuing, modifying or terminating this convention. This review will be completed later this year.

subtopic: INQUIRIES RESPECTING U.S. MODIFICATIONS OF TAX IMPOSED

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON MOSCOW CONFERENCE
speechtext: I should like to direct my question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON MOSCOW CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman will recall that during the past ten days there have been a number of questions on this subject, one by the hon. member for Medicine Hat last week. I indicated the general attitude of the government of Canada toward talks in which we were not a direct participant but about which we have, as every member in this house has an understandably vital interest. These talks are taking place among the United Kingdom, the United States and the Soviet union. Canada is not a participant in these talks which have to do with a proposed agreement with regard to certain aspects of nuclear testing; neither is France, nor are other countries of the international community.
When agreement is reached among the three participants there will be an opportunity to evaluate the effect of the agreement.

Inquiries of the Ministry Its implications will be discussed in the council of NATO. Canada has already, as I have previously intimated, given an outline of its views with regard to the desirability of a complete or partial nuclear test ban. Until such time as we have a full statement I can say no more than I have already. We believe it would be in the interests of the peace of the world that there should be a nuclear test ban. We hope it may go beyond the three areas mentioned and we will follow with interest any other proposals which have to do with the current discussions.

speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON MOSCOW CONFERENCE
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has already asked that question and has received a rather effective answer.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON MOSCOW CONFERENCE
speechtext: I should like to ask the Secretary of State, in view of his reply and the tremendous importance of this test ban treaty to Canada, and in view of the fact that a press report says that Mr. Rusk had a draft test ban agreement that he presented to the senate, whether Canada had a copy of the draft treaty at which the government could look.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON MOSCOW CONFERENCE

Mr. Speaker, I have a question I would like to direct to the Minister of Fisheries, notice of which I have given. I wonder whether the

subsubtopic: STRIKE BY FISHERMEN AND ALLIED WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for sending me notice of his question, which was handed to me on my way down to the chamber. However, I wish to report that I have been kept continuously informed on the situation since a strike was declared on Saturday, July 13 affecting 10,000 British Columbia salmon net fishermen and allied workers. On Friday last the negotiations broke down between the fisheries association of British Columbia and the united fishermen and allied workers union. While realizing that a dispute of this nature comes under provincial jurisdiction, I sent a telegram to both parties suggesting that every possible action be taken to bring price and wage negotiations to a successful conclusion, and resume operation as soon as possible.
On Monday of this week an agreement was reached with the Prince Rupert co-op. affecting 600 to 700 fishermen, who resumed their fishing operation at once. Yesterday, realizing that the loss to the British Columbia economy had already reached the vicinity of $4 million and could lead to a total loss of $12 million to $14 million, I sent a second telegram to both parties expressing my concern about the present and future economy of the fishing industry unless every effort were made to reach a settlement. 1 further suggested that I would welcome reference to proper authorities in order to bring about action necessary to reach agreement.
In reply to the second part of the hon. member's question, I wish to clarify this advice and particularly my reference to proper authorities. The united fishermen and allied workers union is certified under the provincial laws of British Columbia as bargaining agent for tendermen and workers in most fishing plants of that province. While they are not certified under the labour laws for bargaining on behalf of fishermen, section 25 of the province of British Columbia fisheries act, chapter 150, revised statutes of British Columbia provides for arbitration procedures, provided they are asked for, and this is agreed by both parties involved. subsubtopic: REPORTED OUTBREAK OF ANTHRAX
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to address a question to the Minister of Agriculture, of which I have sent him notice. It arises out of a further outbreak of anthrax in buffalo herds in the Northwest Territories. What is being done to eradicate this disease and, more important, to prevent its spread to domestic animals and the human population?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harry W. Hays (Minisier of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: REPORTED OUTBREAK OF ANTHRAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would first like to thank the hon. member for sending me notice of his question. The recent outbreak of anthrax in the Northwest Territories is in the Fort Smith area and is similar to the larger outbreak a year ago.
Anthrax is a reportable disease under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, and the health of animals branch of the Department of Agriculture has a veterinary officer in the area working with the northern affairs wildlife people on control measures. Anthrax does not spread from animal to animal but is a soil borne disease. Animals become infected by picking up the organism from the soil. Once the organism is established in the soil it may exist there for many years.
There are periodic outbreaks of anthrax in other areas of Canada, and in these cases the safe disposal of infected carcasses and the cleaning and disinfection of the infected premises are supervised by department veterinarians, and at the same time other cattle on infected premises are vaccinated. The department, under the provisions of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, is attempting to institute these same principles of control in the Fort Smith area. All infected carcasses are being buried. Attempts have been made to keep the buffalo out of the infected zone, and last fall attempts were made to burn off the infected area in order that buffalo would not return to it.
I might say further, Mr. Speaker, that I do not know whether you have ever had anything to do with the buffalo, but he is a pretty wild bird; and if we could get the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Horner) to use the lariats he was talking about recently to rustle them, then I think we could vaccinate them.

Mr. Chairman, when we adjourned last night, I was saying that the budget introduced by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) has spread confusion, anxiety and suspicion in all classes of our society. Today, I would like to discuss a few articles published in certain papers in order to prove my argument: for instance, in Granby's La voix de I'Est we find in an editorial dated July 6, 1963, that the Minister of Finance was harshly criticized on three points. The first title says, for instance:
Mr. Gordon has to give up 11 per cent tax.
And the text of the article says, among other things:
For that tax imposed on investments and production is prohibitive and harmful, the more so as it will be applied at a time when new investments in industry and business and an increase in production are needed to develop our economy and fight unemployment.
And under this second title:
Violent protests.
[Mr. Pearson.!
We find this and I quote:
Quebec hydro will have to pay an additional $66 million over the next five years. The Quebec government would also see a large increase in its expenditures due to its large investments.
And a third title:
An incompetent minister.
We find this:
This tax is, in fact, a very heavy burden for governments and businessmen. It discourages all investment, even of the most essential nature. Being an obstacle to the expansion plans of the provincial and municipal administrations, it practically leaves no possibility to businessmen to compete with foreign production.
Well, Mr. Chairman, those were the remarks found in the newspapers about the budget submitted by the hon. Minister of Finance, which, according to the minister's own words, was supposed to give some impetus to allow for the progress of Canadian business and industry.
I have here a communication addressed to the Minister of Finance by the Canadian shoe manufacturers association:
Allow us to voice the deep concern of the Canadian shoe industry about the serious effects of your decision to extend the 11 per cent tax to machinery, equipment and industrial supplies.
Faced with keen competition and increased imports of foreign shoes, our Canadian manufacturers have been able to maintain the price of shoes, even though their profits have dwindled.
The new sales tax will considerably increase our costs and the price of shoes will soon reflect the new federal tax.
I could easily go on for quite a while, and quote other newspaper stories, blaming the stand taken by the hon. Minister of Finance during his budget speech, on June 13.
However, I shall be content to quote the headlines of articles by Mr. Laurent Lauzier, in La Presse. On July 6, 1963, his headline was:
A new period of uncertainty.
On the 16th, he wrote:
A rather gloomy prospect.
Again, on the 19th, his headline ran:
The situation is deteriorating.
And so forth. Mr. Chairman, these are comments on a budget which was going to give Canada, or so we were told, a new look. It was going to open up new foreign markets, create new jobs and cure unemployment.
However, having carefully studied the various observations bearing on the tax levied by the hon. Minister of Finance, we are led to believe that far from creating new job opportunities, the measures submitted by the minister will, to the contrary, breed unemployment.

On that matter, I should like to read into the record what the leaders of one of our labour unions, namely the Canada building workers' federation, said in a letter sent to the Minister of Finance. I quote:
To lay out a nine point plan to fight unemployment and at the same time undermine the foundation of the industry in which large projects can be carried out to fight unemployment would only mean to run around in circle, in a vicious circle. The building workers' federation is conscious of the present situation of the national economy and does not believe that your proposal is likely to improve it.
There, Mr. Chairman, you have people who certainly know what they are talking about because they are involved in the building industry and who can also appreciate the effects of the imposition of the new tax, even if it is relaxed or applied gradually.
And what about the reaction of provincial, municipal and school authorities concerning this tax? At this stage, may I recall the remarks made by the Quebec minister of natural resources when he learned about the imposition of that new tax. He passed a very severe judgment on the proposal, stating that it would lead to increased costs and would hamper progress in the province of Quebec.

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, last evening when the hon. member for Waterloo North was speaking I drew the attention of the Chair to the fact that it was quite outside the rules of the house for a member to read documents and newspaper articles that reflect upon the proceedings of the current session of the house. I did not press the matter at the time because the hon. member for Waterloo North, like myself is a backbencher. But what has happened this afternoon, as happened yesterday afternoon in the case of the hon. member for Ontario, is that speeches are being made based almost entirely upon articles which members have read from various newspapers or on letters that have been directed to certain individuals.
I think it is an understood proposition in the House of Commons that a member is elected to represent every section of the economy within his riding and is certainly to receive representations from each, but he is not here to be the voice of every special interest before the House of Commons.
What a point of order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
The member himself is to prepare his own speech and to present it to
Excise Tax Act
the house. If what I am saying requires proof, Mr. Chairman, I would refer to chapter III, rules of debate, in Beauchesne, fourth edition, citation 149 reads as follows:
Besides the prohibitions contained in standing order 35 it has been sanctioned by usage both in England and in Canada that a member, while speaking, must not:
(1) read from a printed document or book commenting on any speech made in parliament during the session.
There are other citations relevant to the hon. member's speech which I might read but I will refer only to paragraph (o), which is in these words:
(o) read from a written, previously prepared speech.
That is also not within the rules. I simply bring that to the hon. member's attention, although I am not making a point of it. Last evening I also read a ruling by Mr. A. E. Ross, acting deputy speaker, made on March 1, 1933 and found on page 802 of Beauchesne, third edition. It is in these words:
It is out of order to quote in committee articles from newspapers commenting on the proceedings then under consideration.
Since the hon. member is a frontbencher I would expect that he would prepare his speech and try to stay within the rules of the house. So I am going to ask the Chair to insist that he do so.

On the point of order, Mr. Chairman.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, the member who just spoke is perhaps the voice crying in the wilderness, because ever since we started consideration of this budget resolution, he has tried constantly to prevent opposition members from commenting on the resolution.
(Text):

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, that is quite improper.
We listened to you. Now you listen to him.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I have not attempted to stop members from doing anything except what is not within the rules of the house. I suggest that the hon. member has no right to reflect upon my intentions because all I am doing is insisting that the rules of the house be followed.
(Translation):

Might I suggest to the hon. member that he study the rules of the house? The hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) who has the floor at

Excise Tax Act
present has obviously the right to quote the comments which were made on this tax. I can understand that this does not suit my hon. friend who has intervened, but I would suggest that when he rises on a point of order or a question of privilege, he should do so for a good reason, not only to distract the chairman or to interrupt the member who has the floor or because he does not agree with his political opinions.
(Text):

On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say to the hon. member that I prepared my own speech and when I was speaking last night I was expressing the opinions not only of thousands of Canadians in my own riding but in all of Canada with regard to the betterment of this country. I was not trying to dictate.
For the withdrawal of the tax.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: I did not suggest that the hon. member for Waterloo North had not prepared his own speech. I do suggest that the hon. member read articles from newspapers and letters addressed to other people in complete contravention of the rules of the house.
You are talking blatant nonsense now.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I recognize that it is necessary at times to support an argument a member is making by reading articles from newspapers if the member wishes to do so. I also recognize the authority cited by the hon. member for Kootenay East. In addition, I have in mind citation 157 in Beauchesne, fourth edition. I am sure the hon. member for Kootenay East will appreciate that this is a very difficult decision for the chairman to make. I would say to the hon. member who is now addressing the committee that it would be pleasing to the Chair if he would refrain from making too many of these quotations, but I understand that he wants to support the argument that he is making.

Mr. Chairman, you will have noted that some time has been taken by this point of order and I trust that allowance will be made for that in deciding when my time runs out. I should like to say to the hon. member for Kootenay East that before trying to lecture somebody else he had better learn his own lessons. He said a while ago that I was reading my speech. I never prepare a text; all I have is a few notes. If he cannot say anything in this house without reading it, then he had better go outside and learn his lessons before he comes here.

I also feel that I am speaking on behalf of somebody, because the mayor of St. Hyacinthe is certainly representing a city of 35,000 people. When I quote members of trade unions or federations or construction associations, they in turn are speaking on behalf of other people. They are all speaking on behalf of someone. If the hon. member for Kootenay East does not know this, then I suggest he sit down and remain silent or learn his lessons before he opens his mouth.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: I am quite happy to receive this lecture from the hon. member.
You deserve it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: However, I want to draw to the attention of the house once more citation 157, despite the fact the chairman overruled my objection, because this still does not give an hon. member licence to read without qualification, and base the major portion of his speech on articles that have been prepared by persons other than the member himself. I believe this is a rule of the house, and if we are going to make honest decisions then we should hear the honest opinions of the members themselves. A member should, in the main, prepare his own speech and not read almost entirely from articles.

You never have to refer to anyone because you have got enough to satisfy your own needs.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, to go on with what I was saying a moment ago, I have here a copy of an item which says that the mayor of St. Hyacinthe called the tax an obstacle and a hindrance to the establishment of industries in the city of St. Hyacinthe.
He was not the only one to make such a remark, as I also have here the opinion of a contractor, Mr. Gaston Maillotte, who heads an important industry in St. Hyacinthe and who stated that, because of that new tax, the building industry will experience a considerable slowing down which will increase unemployment in the months to come.
I also have here a communication from the knitwear union of St. Hyacinthe, which wanted to put in a protest to protect its members. When something is said on behalf of 450 employees and if we take for granted that each one has an average family of three persons, this means a good many tax-paying citizens-I think it represents a great number of people.
I also received a great number of letters of protest against such unfair imposition of industry. For instance, Mr. Benoit Lainesse

wrote me to say that the considered enlargement of his industry, which was to give work to at least 10 more employees or so, has necessarily been postponed, because he cannot, at this time, afford the luxury of additional taxation.
All that, Mr. Chairman, to remind you that when presenting his budget, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) stated that he would give a new impetus to our economy and fight unemployment by imposing a 30 per cent tax on foreign purchases of Canadian securities.
Since then, all we have learned from the Minister of Finance is that during the coming year, the best that the Liberal government can do-we must not forget their rash promises during the election campaign-is to foresee a 5 per cent increase in the gross national product. If we consider that in 1962 there was an 8 per cent increase, then we can say to the magicians in front of us that they have much to learn from their predecessors and that they might well use the methods of the Conservative party during its six years in office.
To regain control over our future. The Minister of Finance has levied, as I said a moment ago, a 30 per cent tax which he withdrew under the pressure of big financial interests in Canada. It should be noted, Mr. Chairman, that it was not as a result of representations from the ordinary citizens that the Minister of Finance yielded, but rather following the protests raised by the mighty.
To fight unemployment. Well, in many industries, as mentioned in a telegram I received from the homebuilders association of the district of Montreal, employers have already been forced to lay off some of their employees and they are also afraid that, sooner or later, they might have to let go of others to whom they would have liked to give work during the winter months.
During the 1961 and 1962 sessions, we heard the Liberal team tell us that they had on file the required programs and projects to get this country moving again as never before, once they were brought back in office, and that those measures would reduce unemployment. And yet, Mr. Chairman, if we look at the statistics for the last two months, we find that unemployment has kept on increasing.
And now what about the world of business? I have with me a report from the newspaper La Presse which tells us that commercial
Excise Tax Act
bankruptcies during the last two months have risen to 200, the highest figure since 1961.
All this is the consequence of a hasty and ill-conceived policy on the part of people who were supposed to transform our country into a Garden of Eden.
Mr. Chairman, after his first mistake, the minister retreated once more when he decided that the tax would be applied progressively, that is from 4 to 8 per cent and then from 8 to 11 per cent. It still remains that building materials, machinery and all the commodities which are used by our industries will be subject to the 11 per cent tax. This will certainly have disastrous effects and far from helping Canada, it will hinder our economic growth and industry in general.
In addition, the progressive introduction of the tax will lead to abuses on the part of unscrupulous speculators.
How could the government prevent speculation on the eve of the day that the tax will pass from 4 to 8 per cent and later when it is increased from 8 to 11 per cent?
Small income earners will certainly be unjustly charged a tax by unscrupulous businessmen and dealers who care only for profits and have no regard for their fellow men.
It is a well known fact, Mr. Chairman, that during the debate no backbencher on the government side has dared state his opinion on this tax. It is obvious that they do not like the tax but they have to toe the party line. They were told: "Shut up. This tax must be levied as we have decided".
During their conversations between themselves, Mr. Chairman, the backbenchers protested against their party policy, but they do not dare say a word because they are afraid of retaliation.
Once again, the team now in office gives evidence that for this political group, the interest of the party comes before that of the country.
We had proof of this during the vote on nuclear arms. All Quebec members, especially, had pledged their word to their constituents that they would object to nuclear arms. However, when the question was put, they were all in favour of them.

Mr. Chairman, I rise
on a question of privilege. The hon. member who has the floor claims that all hon. members who represent the province of Quebec on this side of the house have declared themselves opposed to nuclear arms during the

Excise Tax Act
last election campaign. As far as I am concerned, I can state that such a statement is false because I, for one, never took a stand against them.

Here is a new admission, Mr. Chairman. It resembles that made last night by a member of the Social Credit party who said that, after seeing the Liberal party in action, he was very sorry he had had anything to do with overthrowing the Conservative government last year. And it is only after seeing the Liberal team now in charge that one realizes how wisely public affairs were run under the previous administration.
Mr. Chairman, I will end my remarks by saying that the confusion that followed the presentation of the budget, the indecision, the withdrawals and the errors that marked the first 60 days of the present government, have led the people of Canada to realize quickly how well they were administered under the government headed by the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker).
I do not hesitate to say that the people are waiting for an opportunity to put their faith once more in the Conservative party, because they now see what the Liberal party can do in office. It is quite a different thing for the Liberal party to administer when in opposition and when in office. That party does very well in opposition but when the time comes to implement its program, that is another story.
Mr. Chairman, as I say, the Canadian people are anxious to have again a Conservative government to lead the country.
(Text):

Mr. Chairman, in speaking about this budget and more particularly paragraph 1 of the excise tax resolution, one can only conclude from the many editorials that have been quoted, and from those that have not been quoted, that it certainly was not a popular way of raising money. In fact the minister admitted this and went on to say that no tax was popular, but this was the best of all evils. In defending it he said he still supported the 11 per cent initially announced, which is now down to 4 per cent but will later rise to 11 per cent.
Perhaps the opposition may take some credit for having it reduced a little for the time being, but this is not enough. The Canadian people want it taken off altogether, and

they have strong reasons. We are told many things by the Liberals before and during the election campaign, but since taking power they have found that some things are hard to do.
While this may not deal strictly with the excise tax, the farmers were told this afternoon that they could forget all about the $3 per bushel for the first 300 bushels of their wheat and the $2 per bushel floor price. Instead they were informed that they will get $1.50 initial payment, the same as last year, and that is all. It is another broken promise, and in a sense the budget is a complete broken promise to the Canadian electorate.
I know the hon. member for Kootenay East is a very careful guardian of the house rules and suggests hon. members obey the rules at all times. Therefore I am not going to quote editorials at length, even though there are many which could be read into the record. However there is an interesting one in today's Globe and Mail. I do not intend to read it all but it says:
The Liberal government rode into power last April 8 on a theme that was summarized by Prime Minister Lester Pearson in the sentence, "I don't think that we should spend a nickel after the election unless it contributes to the expansion of the economy."
That one sentence is sufficient to define the point I am trying to make, that expansion of the economy was what the government wanted. Therefore we must ask ourselves how this first paragraph of the resolution will aid in the expansion of the economy.
During the election campaign we were told that the economy was stagnating, and that, even though it had a growth rate of 8 per cent last year, this was not sufficient. However the budget now forecasts a 5 per cent increase in the gross national product. Is this bringing us out of the stagnation of the economy? Certainly people across the country who are giving some thought to the economy do not think so. Certainly the general public who went out to buy lumber after June 13, when this budget resolution was immediately implemented by lumber dealers, do not think so. In fact they said they would not buy lumber or cement.
What did the Canadian Chamber of Commerce have to say about it? This, Mr. Chairman, is a body which generally issues wise and carefully thought out statements. This appears in the July 5 edition of Time magazine. I will read just one brief sentence:
The Canadian Chamber of Commerce said the tax would hurt Canadian sales abroad and slow the pace of the economy.

That is it, in one brief sentence. This will hurt and slow the pace of the economy. This is an economy slowed down by a Liberal government which promised the electorate before April 8 that, because the economy was not moving fast enough, they would speed it up. They have done nothing to speed it up. This resolution, in particular, does nothing to speed it up. It is all well and good for the hon. member for Leeds to say, as he did last evening, why should not the building trades be taxed the same as all other trades in Canada. This to me was a rather irresponsible question. It shows what little thought they gave to the employment problem of this country; it shows what little thought they gave to economic conditions facing Canada today, with a greater increase in the labour force occurring every year.
We must be prepared to move in the proper direction so that these people can expect a better position in life in Canada, so they can expect a job in Canada. We must move in the direction of creating those jobs. Where, I ask you, Mr. Chairman, can a person look for work? Where can a person going out into the labour force today be expected to find a job more easily than in the building trades and the building industry across Canada generally? This is where the greatest growth rate in employment has been over the past two years, and it will continue to be, because Canada is a growing nation. We are a growing nation in spite of this budget and in spite of this tax on the building industry of Canada.
We have heard some talk about deficits and what a terrible thing is deficit budgeting. This was said yesterday by members of the Social Credit party to my right. They went on at great length to say what a terrible thing is a deficit budget and they realize this is a deficit budget. They voted for it, and they agreed that the minister should implement new taxes. I am glad they voted for this tax because they will have to return to the electorate of Alberta some day, and perhaps to the electorate of Quebec. Also, the government of the day will have to return to the electorate and explain to them that they wanted Canada to grow, but taxed the very growth they wanted. It is, and will be, a diminishing tax. Coming back to the question of deficits, Mr. Chairman, I would like to quote some figures from the Canada Year Book of 1962, page 1038. The net debt per capita for each of the years 1952 to 1956 was well over $700, ranging all the way from $773
Excise Tax Act
to $701. From 1957 to 1961 it was well under $700, being approximately $650 per capita. This explains whether there was or was not a growth in net debt. Certainly we have had deficit budgets. This was part of a policy to develop Canada; it was aimed at promoting economic growth to the extent of the 8 per cent which we were finally able to achieve. We brought in a devaluated dollar in 1962, which they criticized. What, in a sense, did that devaluated dollar do? I know, as a member from western Canada, that it aided the general agricultural picture in that area. It also aided the manufacturers in eastern and western Canada; in fact, throughout Canada.
Quoting from page 1472 of Hansard, the Minister of National Revenue had this to say in explaining this particular budget resolution. This is to be found almost at the top of the left hand column:
1 should point out that it is a manufacturers' tax-
I think those brief words explain what we are debating today. It is a manufacturers' tax. Where, I ask you, Mr. Chairman, does Canada hope to achieve the required growth in employment today? We must industrialize; this has been said from one end of the country to another. We must increase employment in our secondary industry and in our manufacturing industry. I ask the committee, in the light of many statements made in this regard, how can the government justify imposing a manufacturers' tax on the manufacturing industry of this budding, young country-
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly. I hope my hon. friend from Renfrew South has learned something about the tobacco industry since the last question he put to me.

I do not smoke, Mr. Chairman. But my question is not about the tobacco industry. I would like to ask the hon. member whether or not his party advocates deficit financing in each year and increasing deficit financing in each year.

This is a rather simple question. Certainly we think a deficit budget is sometimes needed. I am prepared to support it and I am certain this party is prepared to support it. If Canada needs development, if Canada needs more jobs, this is the time and place for deficit budgeting. But we have heard a great deal of talk about indecision, the stalemate the country is in and how things had come to a complete standstill. What about the last three months? Every paper you picked up in the last three months said the country was in a state of flux because

Excise Tax Act
industry did not know what to do about the 11 per cent tax or the 30 per cent tax. I look at today's Globe and Mail. The headline is, "And prices go up and down". This article says:
The bond market moved up and down, like a yo-yo-
How long has it been doing this? It has been doing it ever since June 13. The bond markets, the stock markets generally have been sluggish and moving up and down like a yo-yo. This article continues:
-in response to statements first by treasury secretary Dillon in Washington and then by finance minister Gordon in Ottawa.
They are in a state of great concern as to where we are going, and certainly when one looks at this resolution he can realize why they are in such a state of great concern, because I say again that the government's own definition of it is that it is a manufacturers' tax. I want the people of Canada to know exactly what it is classified as; it is classified as a manufacturers' tax. This is what the Minister of National Revenue, when explaining it, pointed out very clearly as is reported at page 1472 of Hansard. It is a manufacturers' tax on manufacturing; I cannot repeat that too often, because I think it explains what this is. This is why I take the strongest exception to it, because it is in secondary and manufacturing industry that I have always thought and hoped Canada would grow to become perhaps an industrial nation in the years ahead.
We have heard a lot of talk about increased spending and increased deficits. There has been some indecision as to whether this tax should apply to hospitals or old folks' homes. It has finally been taken off schools and universities. Why not take it off churches and municipal buildings. Why not take it off all non-profit buildings?
And libraries.

Yes, and libraries. The hon. member for Leeds, since my speech and the one yesterday by the hon. member for London, has changed his mind and now agrees with me and says, why not take it off everything.

On a point of privilege, Mr. Chairman, I by no means have changed my mind. I think it is a basic proposition that essentially one strives to tax equitably and equally; and in a competitive system, when you pick out one sector and give it special treatment there must be a compelling reason for so doing. My intervention last night was addressed to this precise point.
Order. I am just wondering what is the question of privilege upon which the hon. member is rising.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member twice, in the course of this debate, referred to my having changed my mind with respect to a question that I raised last night. I think it is proper and fitting, in the circumstances, to remind the committee exactly what my interjection was. I do not take it back-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I understand the point that is being made by the hon. member for Leeds. Perhaps there is no point of privilege there. I am wondering whether just saying that an hon. member has changed his mind justifies raising a question of privilege. My suggestion would be that the hon. member for Acadia be allowed to continue his remarks.

I want to assure the hon. member for Leeds that he should not feel self-conscious about changing his mind, because in recent days many hon. members on that side of the house have been changing their minds, particularly since June 13. Perhaps we on this side are encouraged by that, because we hope to have many hon. members on that side change their minds, and particularly the Minister of Finance, in connection with resolution No. 1.
Mr. Chairman, my point of privilege was that I have not changed my mind, and I do not intend to change my mind on this matter. I am against continuing and growing deficits.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member for Leeds, who knows the rules of the house so well, realizes that if he wants to make the point he is now making under the guise of a question of privilege, he will have his opportunity in committee when this speech is concluded.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I know of the hon. member's continuing interest in the Liberal party and his secondary interest in Canada, and perhaps he will take part in the debate and explain the statement made last night which appears on page 2556 of Hansard.
When this resolution was first implemented a great hue and cry rose across the country. Time magazine of last week reported that the minister received, on the average, 350 protests a day regarding this resolution. They were protests from all walks of life. This is what Time magazine says, and I will paraphrase it because the hon. member for Kootenay East does not like to hear people reading from magazines. The hon. member can read it if he likes. The minister can

also deny it if he wants to. I accept what I read and I accept this statement. Some 350 letters and telegrams are sent to the Minister of Finance each day, mainly on this particular resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question. I presume they include the telegrams which were heartily in favour of this particular way of raising revenue?

This is a very interesting interjection from the minister. He seems to be capable of making interjections which deepen himself in the well in which he has sunk since June 13. I would ask the minister right now to tell us how many are in favour, or to produce the copies of the ones he has received in favour of this particular resolution. Let the house and the country decide whether or not, on his particular Gallup poll, this resolution has found favour. As I said in my opening remarks, a great hue and cry has been raised across the country against this particular tax. The resolution ended by saying that all agricultural machinery would be exempt, and all farm buildings or buildings on anyone's property would have to be taxed.
Then on July 8 the minister reduced the tax to 4 per cent, and said, "Catch as catch can". He told the people they can collect from the retailers the other 7 per cent they had paid. He said that if they had bought a house he was sure that the builder would be a good fellow and return the $500 to $1,500 which this 7 per cent tax would represent. But he did not offer, nor did the Department of National Revenue, to see to it that this tax would be returned.
Would the hon. member permit a question? Would he mind repeating what he said about the effect of the 11 per cent tax?

If I recall my remarks I said that the 11 per cent would amount to between $500 and $1,500 on the average house purchased since June 13, and if the minister would like to dispute that I will be glad to listen to him.
I think the hon. member realizes he is in error there.

No, I had not realized that. I was informed of that by my constituents. If a person bought a house for $7,000, then 11 per cent would be well over $700. That is it in a nut shell. This has happened to constituents of mine who produced the figures and facts. They have been charged $700 on a $7,000 house. I told them they would get that back and they asked me how. I said I would look into it and try and find the
Excise Tax Act
proper way. But I am sorry to say that I have not been able to ascertain for certain how this particular constituent of mine will get back in excess of $700 tax paid, owing to the indecision and the retreating change of mind of the Minister of Finance.
We talked of indecision in the April 8 election campaign. This country has never seen 90 days of more indecision and mumbling and more state of influx of the economy. As the Leader of the Opposition stated, there was a statement made by the United States government some time ago about a pat on the head at Hyannis Port, and a kick to the Canadian economy. We have received more kicks to the economy in the last 90 days than we have ever received at any time in past history.
What about the "state of influx"?

The constituency of Renfrew South is in a state of influx. We have heard talk about home construction in this resolution, yet two or three days before the budget the Minister of Labour stated that $500 would be given to new home construction started in the winter time. Everybody thought: "Oh boy, this is a real handout". It had nothing to do, of course, with the statement of the leader of the government in today's Globe and Mail, in which he referred to no more give-aways. He summarized the theme of the April 8 election in one sentence, and I want to repeat it because it is a good one to repeat often to those now embarked upon give-aways of one sort or another, to undo the harm they did with the other hand, one might say. He said:
I do not think we should spend a nickel after the election unless it contributes to the expansion of the economy.
In what way does $500 toward home construction in the wintertime offset this tax of something like $700 on a home, whether it is built in the winter or the summer? In what way does $500 on a home built in the wintertime compensate for construction in the wintertime? I have received many telegrams opposing this gift of $500 toward home construction. What does it do? It does not offset this tax. According to the Minister of Labour's own admission in this house it does not do that. What it does is to take $500 off the value of every home already built, and it taxes those same home owners so as to pay for the $500 the government is willing to give new home builders in the wintertime.
This business of the right hand giving one thing and the left hand taking a little more back, Mr. Chairman, certainly reminds an old farmer like myself of driving two balky horses and getting nowhere-one trying to go ahead

Excise Tax Act
and one back. I am sure many hon. members, particularly the Minister of Agriculture, have witnessed or endured the task of trying to get somewhere with a team of horses like that. I suggest to the Liberal party that they should get together to get rid of the balky horses, because one cannot have an economy which will grow and provide all the jobs needed by the people who are newly entering the labour force unless everyone is pulling together and every measure introduced is designed to secure a better growth rate in Canada-a rate of growth even faster than the 8 per cent we had in 1962. It may be that the dismal efforts in these resolutions account for the minister not forecasting an increase of more than 5 per cent during the present year, but I hope Canadians will have enough faith in their country to invest in it and enable our gross national product to grow fast enough to absorb those who are added to our labour force every day.
The minister has reduced this tax from 11 per cent to 4 per cent.
No. He has not reduced it. He has amortized it.

The minister has tried to clear up certain of these definitions. I know that many items of interest to agriculture are taxed, as things now stand, but I hope the definitions will be further clarified and that the taxes can be reduced in the months ahead. Agricultural buildings and all buildings put up by non-profit organizations should be exempt. Church buildings as well as schools and universities should be exempt. Certainly, we should not tax the generous gifts and donations made to these worthy institutions. We should at least move in the direction of allowing such things as these to grow and flourish. There is a place in Canada for churches, religions and libraries. We should be big enough to allow them to be free of the particular building tax which is now proposed.
The minister may sit and smile about his conceited ideas as to how Canada should grow. I have not written any book on how it should grow but I have had some definite ideas. We see in Time magazine that even the Prime Minister at one time questioned his great economic adviser, the Minister of Finance. He asked him: "Have you lost confidence in yourself?" The minister replied: "No, I have taken so many knocks during my 57 years that I can take one more". Well, the hon. gentleman has taken a good many knocks since June 13. I do not want to be the final straw or anything like it, but I do wish to say that the committee should give serious consideration to measures such as this which

will hinder or halt the rate of economic growth in Canada, which is so vital to a young country such as ours.
Once again, I would ask this government to correlate its actions and its thoughts. Some time ago we heard a lot of talk about unemployment. Hon. members opposite said it was the primary concern of our country. Well, unemployment seems to have been replaced in these days by balance of payments problems. As I say, I hope the government will correlate its thinking and its actions so that our rate of economic growth is at least as high as it was last year. That is what I look forward to. But I do not think it will come about, and that is why I am strongly opposed to these resolutions.
We have gathered that.
Hon. members over there can laugh and smile. They will have to face the public sooner or later. That is the great thing about politics. Sooner or later they will have to face the music.
Not worse than listening to you.
They can make all sorts of snide remarks, but I believe the public is fully aware of what this tax means. It is a manufacturers' tax which is unwanted and unwarrantable in Canada today.

I do not wish to take up the time of the committee for too long but in view of the amiable remarks of the hon. member for Acadia I feel I should intervene briefly.
I think it is clear that the purpose of this budget is twofold. The first intention is to stimulate the economy, but in order to do this we have to meet the obligations of the country. We, as a party, have to do this whether we want to do it or not. Looking at the white paper, I find, as set down on page 68, that we are now paying 14 per cent by way of public debt charges. Following the interesting series of speeches which were read into the record last night in connection with this matter, I put a question on the order paper. I have not yet had an answer to this question, but the question relates to federal, provincial and municipal debt in Canada and the servicing charges in connection therewith. I am old fashioned enough to think that some day we shall have to pay for these continuing deficits. It would be delightful if we could always be in the position in the business cycle where we could apply

Why did you make all those promises, then.

I earnestly believe we will have to face these debts some time and I am surprised that in the old Conservative party not one voice has been raised since this parliament was called to express concern about whether we shall ever balance our budget.

None of us likes these taxes. There is not a Liberal member in the house who has not had on his desk letters, telegrams and notes of telephone calls from constituents disturbed by these budget suggestions.

Mr. Chairman, I think that the hon. member for Leeds is straying from the subject. He is reviving a subject that has been dealt with before, and that is not within the purview of this debate.
The suggestion of impropriety has gone by the boards. Now the suggestion is that the minister is a jackass or does not know where to tax. I am very sorry that any additional taxes had to be imposed.
So are we.

May I ask hon. members, what is discreditable about placing the equipment and supplies and construction materials industries in precisely the same position as other industries? I wish we could have avoided this tax. It would have helped me very much with some of my friends and constituents. But if a tax has to be imposed, does it not make sense that at least we should deal equitably with all sections of industry? Surely the Conservative party in their economic philosophy must entertain some kind of support for the proposition of maintaining competitive enterprise. Competitive enterprise surely means the interplay of the market forces, supply and demand. Any time we intervene by way of a tax law and make changes to stimulate one sector of the economy as against another, or one area of a sector of the economy as against others, we create some kind of distortion. Surely at times we do that because, as the hon. member for Acadia said, there are areas where such stimulus does in fact do some economic good.
Perhaps it is in the secondary manufacturing sector where there is a large element of labour in relation to production. In these areas, of course, we are deeply concerned about employment. But surely as a basic proposition it makes sense that in our economy we should strive to deal equitably and fairly with all areas. If additional tax had to be imposed, does it not seem just and reasonable that at least the tax gaps should be filled?
I have not heard yet in any of the contributions of Conservative members any suggestion as to where, alternatively, they would have liked the additional tax to be imposed. Is it their proposition that it should have been in the form of additional income tax? Should it be by way of still higher sales tax elsewhere? Should it be in the form of higher tariffs?

You are the government.

We are the government, but I am outside the establishment. I am just a private member of parliament. But I am deeply concerned about the fact that in less than six years we have accumulated deficits in excess of $2.9 billion. It seems to me that at some time we are going to have to pay for these deficits, just as I think that at some time we are going to have to pay for the cost of fighting world war II.
We have heard speeches by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, the financial critic for the New Democratic party. He spoke very cleverly on this matter. I do not subscribe to his economic theories but essentially they are that we are living in a neo-Keynesian world where we do not have to consider balancing budgets any more. These responsibilities do not enter into his philosophy, which is apparently that we can live in a continual state of deficit financing. Perhaps he does not go quite that far, but the implication is there; and I certainly recall that the leader of the New Democratic party said something very similar. He suggested that respected economic opinion today suggests that we do not need to worry about balancing our accounts any more. I happen to be old-fashioned enough to think we do and that if we actually spend more than we bring in by way of revenue essentially we are in trouble.
The armed forces are an illustration of this. I am not going to digress but I simply wish to give the facts. In the last six years we have actually failed to equip our army, navy and air forces properly. They have tended to fall down and down in the ratio of equipment to manpower. This is what is happening in our economy with regard to replacing our capital, and worse still even to the extent of not meeting our debt obligations.
I do not subscribe to everything Social Credit members say, but they are right in emphasizing the added burden to Canadians of debt charges. These debt charges are growing sharply. Considering our small population, this is a burden, and I am with the Minister of Finance in any form of discipline that needs to be imposed on the Canadian economy to make competitive enterprise more competitive and to allow us to move into the world economy with our heads held high, as I think we must do.
I am not going to carry on further. I do not like this tax. I do not think there is one member on our side who does; but before these deliberations are finished I should like to hear some suggestions from the Conservatives, an old party which I always thought believed in the principle of conserving- "conserving", meaning to save, to keep, to protect, to hold, to husband. I do not see

much sign of that in their economic philosophy, and I should like to see some evidence of it. I should like to see some of their members suggest where and how we are going to conserve Canada for the future along the lines that I think have been indicated by the Minister of Finance.

Mr. Chairman, I would not like the discussion of the budget resolutions to be concluded without making a few remarks, for, once again, it has been proved that taxes are never popular, so that the 11 per cent tax on building materials, which the Minister of Finance announced in his budget speech on June 13 last, raised such a flood of protest on all sides, that the minister had to make us swallow it in stages.
As far as I am concerned, I received letters and telegrams of protest from all parts of the country, and more particularly from my riding. Anyway, I find myself that the home building industry is the most affected by the new tax, because it directly affects those who were planning to build a home or, as the case may be, to make some renovations.
As that new tax will slow down any new building activity as well as repair work in existing property, construction workers will inevitably find it more difficult to find employment in that industry.
Those who, directly or indirectly, are responsible for the marketing of building materials, as well as those who normally look after their transportation, will also be hit by the tax.
Mr. Chairman, for a number of years we have been facing this serious problem of unemployment, which, instead of diminishing, is getting worse, more particularly in the province of Quebec. As a matter of fact, the last figures which were submitted to us indicate that unemployment has increased in an alarming fashion during the month of June 1963, in comparison to June 1962.
We believe that instead of interfering with the normal progress of the building industry, the government should use appropriate steps, such as fiscal incentives or other means to promote it.
Why discourage those who intended to become home owners in the near future? And why forget the old adage: activity in the building trade is a sign of prosperity?
A great deal was made of the $500 bonus this government intends to grant those who will build during the four less favourable months of the year. Now, Mr. Chairman, I

myself am a construction worker, and I know that it is much more expensive to build during the winter months. As a matter of fact, it is necessary to heat the water and the aggregate for the foundations of new buildings. It is necessary also to surround the house with a temporary shelter to keep out the cold. All this causes additional costs in housing construction, not to mention the fact that the workers do not work in comfort during the winter months. Consequently, this $500 bonus is greatly reduced because of the increased costs of construction.
Mr. Chairman, I also note that this new 11 per cent tax on building materials does more to cancel that bonus than any other tax.
Mr. Chairman, every family is entitled to a decent shelter, and it has been established that he who owns a small plot of land is more eager to defend his country against subversive doctrines, because he owns a share in his country. We need accommodation everywhere. Our cities, villages and rural areas are full of slums that we must plan to replace as soon as possible, because, after all, human beings should be better sheltered than animals.
The area I represent will be seriously affected by this tax, particularly on account of the tornado which hit the region at the end of June with indescribable force, specially in a part of the provincial riding of Abitibi West, spreading death and desolation.
In fact, over 350 farmers in 15 localities suffered losses. Barns, sheds and houses were torn down, and those buildings must be reconstructed.
Last July 3, I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) whether he considered exempting from the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials those who had suffered from that tornado. At that time, he answered that he would have a statement to make on Monday, July 8. We must realize that without assistance, even if they are full of good will, most of them will not be able to recover from the losses suffered because of that tornado.

The budget has been meeting with such an opposition that the Minister of Finance cannot indefinitely continue to put up with our sick monetary system. He will have to adopt the monetary theory of the Social Credit party, for it is impossible to go on governing the country with taxes and loans as it is done now.
Since confederation we have had 72 budgets showing a deficit. Seventy two out of 96. Those budgets left with us a gigantic debt of $24,182 million, as can be seen on page 124 of the public accounts for 1962-63. That debt will force us to pay this year the amount of $882 million in interest only. That is enough to make us think.
The Minister of Finance should use the Bank of Canada to finance the government's expenses rather than following a policy of taxes and loans. We would thus have a balanced economic policy for all Canadians.

This afternoon and during the various stages of the budget debate, we have heard quite a number of economic theories. Economic theories, of course, can be varied
