depending, I suppose, upon whether one follows the London school of economics, the Harvard school, the Chicago school or some other school.
And the Leeds school.

Yes, as the hon. member for Port Arthur mentions, the Leeds school. A few moments ago the hon. member for Leeds suggested that no one on this side of the house had made any suggestion as to the alternative method the Minister of Finance might have used to raise the necessary funds to cover the government's increased expenses. Well, in a few moments I will be pleased to offer some suggestions to which some consideration might be given. In addition to that, I was rather surprised by the request for suggestions by the hon. member for Leeds because I recall that a few months ago his party was the one that was supposed to have all the answers. This does not seem to have proven to be the case.
This question of deficit financing was mentioned by the hon. member for Leeds. I do not believe this is exactly the place to get into an argument on the economic theories of public finance. However, there did seem to me to be some confusion in the hon. member's mind as to the difference between external debt of the country and internal debt. However, be that as it may, a great deal has been said about this 11 per cent sales tax on building materials. I feel that to date practically everything that could be said has been said, and I do not wish to take up the time of the committee by reiterating what has already been said.
My only comment is that I was interested to hear the Minister of Finance say this afternoon that he had received letters of commendation on this tax. I find that interesting, and I say I am quite sure that none of them came from the part of the country I happen to represent. It is quite true that this sales tax of 11 per cent on building materials has been altered to some degree by the minister and is now being imposed on the instalment plan. I suppose one might refer to that as paralysis of industry by instalments rather than in one fell swoop.
As I said, many comments have been made on this subject and, apart from the fact that I agree thoroughly with the criticism of this tax, that is all I wish to say in that regard.
As I recall it, the Minister of Finance said in one of his speeches that this tax now being imposed on building materials and production machinery was being imposed on these items because they had been exempted to date, and for that reason it was only fair that they be taxed. This was the implication I gathered

from the minister's remarks. On the face of it, if one has to raise additional revenue, it sounds very reasonable; but it is not as reasonable as it sounds.
The building and secondary manufacturing industries have not paid this tax over the years, and as a result have become adjusted to not paying it in relation to the rest of the economy. To use the ordinary term, they are what might be called vested interests and have become adjusted to our taxation system as it existed until now, and of course to our various customs tariffs.
The economy could be likened to a pile of bricks. If you pull out two or three of the important and largest bricks you disturb the whole pile and all the others have to readjust themselves into a new heap. If you start shifting around one or two of the major props to the economy this has effects and ramifications all through the economy, and by changing the tax structure with respect to these industries you unsettle the whole economy.
Secondary industry, which is the type we must depend on for further development of the economy, has had a bit of a boost during the last year or two, largely as a result of the revalued dollar, both with respect to imports and the developing export business. However I feel I must ask the minister for some clarification of what secondary industry will pay in the form of this new taxation. There is already a great deal of confusion in secondary industry, and if the hon. member for Kootenay East does not object I should like to quote from two letters with respect to the tax.
The letters are from two very large secondary industries, in one case from the general manager and in the other from the owner. One is a machine tool industry which employs close to 1,000 people, and I might say in passing that all industry is not located in Montreal or Toronto, as we are sometimes led to believe in this house. The other is a large manufacturer of automobile parts and aluminum tubes.
The first letter is from Standard Tube and T.I. Limited in Woodstock, and it says in part:
Our company is constantly in competition with United States on fabricated tubular products, particularly in the automotive industry. On many occasions, equipment and tooling involved for Canadian production is costly and the imposition of 11 per cent sales tax may well cause us to lose potential business. In effect, imported parts are now given a substantial cost advantage over Canadian made parts.
In conjunction with other automotive parts manufacturers, we have recently entered into certain reciprocity contracts involving export of materials to the United States. Here again, the 11 per cent sales tax now represents an extremely serious obstacle to the furtherance of such badly needed export business.
Already we have been obliged to review our capital outlay budget. Of necessity, certain items

must either be cancelled or delayed as the additional tax involved on production machinery causes us to exceed original and approved estimates.
The other letter is from Mr. Harold Wilson, who is general manager, and I believe principal owner, of the Morrow Screw and Nut Company Limited, which is a very large machine tool company. He says:
I feel the situation as regards the 11 per cent sales tax is going to be not only intolerable but very disastrous to our industry. As I think I said before, any increase in our costs can only be reflected in loss of the new export market which we have begun to develop and even greater losses in our own domestic market. In connection with our parent organization, the Ingersoll Machine and Tool Company, it would appear that we may be faced with the loss of major portions of our steering gear business as the automobile manufacturers compare our prices against laid down prices from their own American plants, and naturally an increase in our price is going to swing the balance towards importation.
I have investigated carefully the clause which seems to re-establish the exemption on materials expended in production. Although at first this was thought to represent some improvement, on more careful study this would appear to be not too great an improvement. As we read the paragraph the exemption is only applied to materials, which I gather are raw materials, which are expended in manufacturing operations. It would appear that this exemption does not apply to other expendable items such as perishable tools. This item of perishable tools alone is one of our most severe manufacturing expenses. The application of the tax to this alone will add a very severe burden to our cost structure. I feel that it is necessary for industry to be supplied with a very careful directive advising how this exemption is or is not applied and to what. The word 'material" just is not good enough to cover all the ramifications of this question.
There seems very little doubt that the imposition of this tax on production materials and machinery used in manufacturing will have a very serious effect on our balance of payments.
In regard to this question of our balance of payments there is one way in which matters could be assisted, and I refer to the question of travel in the wintertime to the West Indies. I think increased subsidies on air fare would help this, and it would certainly help our balance of payments if the commercial banks in Canada were advised to recommend the purchase of travellers cheques in Canadian funds instead of American dollars, to people visiting countries other than the United States. This is something which could be done in every branch of every bank.
I think everybody will agree with the minister when he said he felt it was necessary to try to raise additional funds to help balance the budget. No one would seriously disagree with that objective, but it is a question of how he might have gone about it. As I recall it, he outlined in his budget speech certain alternatives to which he had given some consideration. One that I recall 28902-5-1651

Mr. Chairman, I am not in the least interested in hearing the comments of the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand. As the hon. member for Leeds was asking for suggestions, I am merely trying to accommodate him and pass on a few. Some hon. members opposite do not wish to hear these suggestions; nevertheless, I am going to continue. There is another method which I think might commend itself to the minister. It is perhaps a different or unusual source of tax revenue. This would be, to evolve a method -and I am sure the minister and his associates could devise some means of doing this -to try and shake loose some of the large funds held by insurance companies, for the purchase of common stocks. As I recall it, insurance companies can invest 15 per cent in common stocks. In the United States they are allowed to invest 25 per cent, but it is 15 per cent in Canada. The information I have is that only 4 per cent of these investments are at the present time in common stocks; the rest are in bonds, mortgages and first mortgage bonds which, compared with good common stocks, have a relatively low rate of return.
If means could be devised-and there are always good tax ways of doing these things -to encourage the loosening up of these funds for investment in common stocks, this would have a threefold effect. First of all, insurance companies have hundreds and hundreds of millions of dollars available for investment, and if this suggestion were put

into effect it would undoubtedly increase the extent of Canadian ownership in Canadian industry. This would be a very good thing in the long run, of course, for our balance of payments problem, in particular with respect to exporting dividends abroad. Second, the increased returns to the companies holding these stocks would provide a higher rate of profit and the Minister of National Revenue would be able to collect more corporation tax. Third, another effect would be that with an increased ownership by these companies of Canadian common stocks, the dividends would be paid into Canadian companies and would be taxable, instead of going abroad and being subject only to the 15 per cent tax.
There are one or two questions I would like to put to the Minister of Finance, and perhaps the Minister of National Revenue, for clarification. Many people are uncertain in this regard, and I have not been able to obtain any clarification on just what goods used in manufacturing and production are to be taxed. Does this apply to such things as sulphuric acid, hydrochloric acid and various solvents used in industry? In some cases these commodities can be used several times. Are these things to be taxed? These are questions manufacturers in secondary industry would like to have answered. My second question is with regard to such items as saws, drills and various pieces of machine tools that are used up in the manufacture of other tools. There is still a great deal of confusion in this regard and perhaps before the resolutions are passed we will obtain some clarification from one of the ministers I have mentioned. I think this would bring back a great deal of confidence on the part of these industries. One of the problems is not so much that they have to pay a tax, because if they have to pay it, they have to pay it; but some of these companies would like to know what they have to pay the tax on. This doubt has created a great deal of delay in planning in secondary industry, which will be very detrimental to our economy. If the Minister of Finance or the Minister of National Revenue could clarify these matters, it would be very helpful indeed.

There are times in this house when I feel very much alone, in view of the fact that I am the only manufacturer of printed material, as far as I am aware, in the House of Commons. When the minister originally introduced his budget he left unanswered a lot of questions in the minds of hon. members, and that goes for the backbenchers on this side of the house as well as members on opposition benches. But subsequently at various stages I think he has cleared up many of these unanswered questions. For instance, the question is asked why, instead of increasing taxes on production machinery he did not increase the income tax. To that question he answered that in his opinion it would have required too drastic an increase to get the required result. He also checked into the possibility of raising the excise tax where applicable to 12 or 13 per cent, but came to the conclusion that again this would hurt the average Canadian. He also investigated the possibility of raising corporation taxes, but found that this obvious source of revenue had been taxed to its capacity. If I am not mistaken he mentioned cigarettes and alcohol, but came to the conclusion that there again further taxation would only result in diminishing returns. The idea of taxing insurance as advocated by the hon. member for Oxford would no doubt result in an increase in insurance premiums which the average Canadian would be called upon to share. I think the danger into which we are falling at the moment, and one I suppose which the Minister of Finance cannot do anything about, is that we are discussing a budget resolution by resolution and forgetting the effects of the budget, good and bad, in the over-all picture.
I should like to deviate from my notes, because time is short, to mention one or two specific things which have occurred in my riding in the last few days. I want

That is another example of the way the budget is helping small industry. I have personally-and I think this is the duty of every hon. member, once he goes home and forgets party politics-found jobs in the last few months for at least 75 people in my riding who are over 45. I received the help of the unemployment insurance commission, and found jobs for people whose unemployment insurance benefits will have run out by the time the winter months set in. As we know, small companies are being encouraged by the grant of a subsidy of, I think, up to $75 a month to hire people over 45. By making this personal canvass in my area I have found jobs for a lot of people, mostly in these small fuel oil firms; and while this may not contribute an awful

lot to our unemployment problem, it is very important that somebody helps people out of work. This is one way in which we can help.
In summing up, Mr. Chairman, while it is the prerogative of the house to scrutinize minutely every stage of the budget, I think in all fairness to the Minister of Finance we should look at the budget as a whole, objectively, take advantage of the provisions for accelerated depreciation and the tax holiday, and accept the fact that basically this is a good budget for Canada.
Mr. Chairman, I have half a minute left to discuss the things I intend to discuss, so would the committee permit me to call it six o'clock.
Agreed.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: It being six o'clock, shall I rise, report progress, and request leave to sit again at the next sitting of the house?

Agreed.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I presume the house leader will tell us that we will go on with the present resolution tomorrow. Supposing we finish it, has he anything else to suggest?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes, sir, I have. We will go on with these resolutions and if they are completed I intend to ask the unanimous consent of the house to proceed immediately with the bills. I hope that might be forthcoming, but I am not asking for that now. We would also take the bill respecting the surcharges and the economic council, and I would think that that would probably occupy us most of the day. If perchance we have a little time in the last hour of the day we could perhaps occupy it with the transport estimates.
As for Friday, I should like to confer with hon. gentlemen opposite before I try to forecast any business for that day.
It being two minutes after six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Thursday, July 25, 1963
